County BZA Approves Slaughterhouse, Auto Repair Requests, Part 1
The Shelby County Board of Zoning Appeals on Tuesday approved requests for a small-scale animal slaughtering operation near Edinburgh and an automotive repair business near Fairland.
The board voted 4-1 to approve a use variance request from Kio Hmung for property at 7781 W 600 S, Edinburgh, allowing a small-scale animal slaughtering service in an agricultural zoning district. Kevin Carson cast the lone dissenting vote.
According to planning documents, the proposal would allow customers to purchase animals for cultural celebrations such as weddings and birthdays and use the property to slaughter and process the animals for personal consumption. The facility would operate primarily on weekends by appointment and serve an estimated two to five customers per week.
The proposal prompted extensive discussion among board members regarding disposal of animal remains, sanitation standards and state oversight. Questions centered on whether carcasses would be removed promptly and what safeguards would be required before the business could begin operations.
Board member Jim Douglas questioned how waste would be handled during warmer months.
“If they’re killing on Saturday and they don’t get picked up until Monday, you’ve got an unsanitary situation,” Douglas said.
The petitioners said they planned to comply with requirements from the Indiana Board of Animal Health and use a rendering or disposal service approved by the state. However, they acknowledged they had not yet finalized a disposal contractor because state licensing requires local zoning approval before the process can move forward.
Planning Director Desiree Calderella noted that the state, not the county BZA, would regulate sanitation, food safety and licensing requirements.
“So really what you’re looking at is, is animal slaughtering in compliance with all regulations appropriate for the property,” Calderella said. “In my opinion, it is, because it’s so isolated.”
The property sits approximately one-third of a mile from the nearest public road and one-quarter mile from the nearest residence.
The board approved the request with a stipulation requiring proof of registration with the Indiana Board of Animal Health before operations may begin.
The board then voted 4-1 to approve a use variance allowing Mitchell Harvey to continue operating a small automotive repair business from a pole barn at 4640 W 700 N, Fairland. Carson cast the lone dissenting vote.
The business had drawn complaints earlier this year after neighboring residents reported increasing vehicle storage on the property. County staff discovered the business advertised online and determined the pole barn had been constructed without permits.
Harvey told the board he built the barn himself after purchasing the property in 2021 and hoped eventually to transition from dealership work into his own repair business.
“I’ve always dreamed of having a pole barn,” Harvey said.
He acknowledged the property had become cluttered while he dealt with health issues and attempted to balance the side business with a full-time job.
“I got overwhelmed,” he said. “Obviously, that’s my fault.”
His father, Mark Harvey, also spoke during the hearing and joked about the petitioner’s claim that he built the barn alone.
“He can say he built it by himself, but I helped him,” Mark Harvey said, drawing laughter from the room.
Mark Harvey also told the board his son had recently battled thyroid cancer while trying to manage the business and organize the property.
“He’s a great kid,” Harvey said. “He’s got the work ethic of a 50-year-old, and he’s only 30.”
Some neighbors supported the request, describing Harvey as a hardworking young business owner who had already begun cleaning up the property after receiving notice from the county. Others objected, saying the business conflicted with the quiet residential character of the area.
County staff had recommended denial, arguing the commercial operation conflicted with surrounding residential uses and that outdoor vehicle storage was highly visible from the roadway.
Despite the recommendation, the board approved the request with several conditions, including limiting outdoor vehicle storage to a designated gravel area behind the home, restricting most gravel parking to four vehicles and limiting operations to the petitioner only with no employees.
Board members also discussed the possibility of Harvey returning in the future to request expanded permissions if the business remains orderly and compliant.
“I feel like maybe we should walk before we run,” Douglas said.

NOTEBOOK:
ANNIVERSARY ANNOUNCEMENT: Steve Thompson and Melanie (Jenkins) Clarke Thompson, Shelbyville, celebrate 38 years of marriage today. They were married May 14, 1988, at Franklin Road Church of Christ, Indianapolis. They have three children, Kari Clarke, Kristi (Clarke) Borchardt (spouse, Eric), and Nicholas Thompson, and three incredible grandchildren.
Fairland Baptist Church will host a rummage and bake sale from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday, May 16, at the church, 102 Meridian St., Fairland. Organizers said proceeds from the event will support the purchase of a handicap-accessible van. Donations for the sale were contributed by more than 10 families, and the event will be held rain or shine.
HOOSIER NEWS: Indianapolis Public Schools will donate seven unused properties to Habitat for Humanity of Greater Indianapolis to support construction of up to 16 affordable homes over the next three years, including potential opportunities for IPS employees seeking homeownership. The initiative comes as district officials say rising housing costs have led some employees to make early withdrawals from retirement accounts. IPS is also partnering with Indianapolis Neighborhood Housing Partnership to provide financial counseling, homeownership education and affordable lending assistance for employees. (Chalkbeat)

This Day in Shelby County History
Local headlines reported on or around this date in Shelby County history. Selections are curated by The Addison Times from Shelby County Public Library Genealogy Department materials.
2016: The second annual Battle of the Bands was held at the Skyline Drive-in Theatre. The event raised money for the Chris Lytle Foundation and the Shelbyville Boys and Girls Club.
2006: Sandy Allen, the world’s tallest woman, spoke at Hendricks Elementary. Students tried on and walked in her size-22 shoes.
Loper Elementary rewarded its top 18 fundraising students with a ride in a stretch Hummer limousine. Students who sold at least $250 worth of candy bars were eligible for the prize.
1996: Morristown’s Jason Smalley, a Triton Central student, won the Blue River Career Programs auto mechanics competition.
The Shelbyville Middle School science team placed fifth among the 206 teams that competed in the junior division of the Hoosier Academic Super Bowl. Team members were Nick Conner, Josh Orem, Allison Siebert, Sarah Nahre, Eric Peters, Ben Dalton, Matt Wimmer, Curtis Gahimer, Andre Jackson, Deacon Marshall, Andrew Carter, Elaine Bogemann, Luke Simons, Andrea Jester and B.J. Griewe. Jim Slater was the coach. The Southwestern Junior-Senior High School interdisciplinary team placed third in the state in the junior division. Team members were Melissa Gaddis, Jeremy McIntire, Sara Nay, Kristen Parmer, Sarah Wells and Christine Trefun.
1986: Shelbyville Central Schools Superintendent Don Strobel said Denny Ramsey, principal at Coulston, would move to Loper as principal to succeed Michael Lindley. Ramsey had been with SCS since 1971, eight years as an elementary teacher at Marion School and seven as principal, first at Pearson, then at Coulston. His wife DeLane was a kindergarten teacher, and their daughter
1976: Shelbyville’s BB shooting team placed second in the state. Team members were April Landwerlen, Eric Farlow, Kevin Elkins, Mike Soller, Cathy Soller, Sherri Soller and Troy Lawver. Wayne Weintraut was the coach.
1966: Triton Central won its first county track championship. Team members were Dave Trickey, Steve Abel, Dave Frey, Ken Dickman, Gary Mallory, Larry Fair, Jerry Trimble, David Hensley, Art Shelton, Jim Trimble, Paul Mohr, Harry Shelby, Steve Banker, Norm Morton, Ron McCalip, Phil Stainbrook, Dennis Crafton, Eddie Herron, Steve Crafton and John Coy. Managers were Danny Holt, Roy Ginn, Roger McNew and David Champa. Art Dobbins was the coach.
1956: Work neared completion on a new concrete block building on the southeast corner of Washington and Noble streets. It would be the new home of Birkhead Heating and Cooling. The former building on the site had been built more than 100 years ago.
1946: Hundreds of Shelby County children, ranging in age from six months to 10 years, had been immunized against diphtheria, Shelby County Medical Society officials reported. The Society had provided free vaccinations for families in need.
1936: Colescott School won first in the Poppy Day school poster contest. Student winners were Francis Cheatham, Gene Riser, Betty Jean Hendrickson, Chester Hamilton, Marion Fox and Claude Hendricks.
Chester Sandman received a postcard carried across the Atlantic Ocean by the Hindenburg. The card was from a potential supplier for Sandman Bros. It had been re-mailed from Lakehurst, New Jersey, where the airship had landed.
1926: City Council ordered a dump truck for use by the Street Department. Floyd Wertz, chairman of the streets and alleys committee, had wanted another truck. He said he would let the new truck stand in the city garage and not be used.

OBITUARIES
Herman Odell Spivey, 82, of Fairland, passed away Monday, May 11, 2026, at Hancock Regional Hospital. He was born Sept. 4, 1943, in Moss, Tennessee, to Herman Spivey and Vella (Etheridge) Spivey.
Herman spent his first 17 years in Celina, Tennessee, and graduated from Celina High School with the Class of 1960. After graduation, he moved to the Fairland area where he met his wife and began to start his family. He was a dedicated employee with General Motors, retiring in 2000 with 30 years and six minutes of service. He specialized as a machinist with the company. Herman had a passion for cars and working on them, especially doing auto body work. He was also an avid NASCAR enthusiast. He enjoyed being outdoors riding his ATV through the trails and even enjoyed being out on his scooter. A couple of his favorite pastimes were drinking with his buddies at the barn and spending quality time with his family at family gatherings.
He married Carol (Wainscott) Spivey on Aug. 14, 1964, and she survives. They shared 61 loving years of marriage together. He is also survived by his daughter, Kim (husband, Bryan) Rice; grandchildren, Dylan (Laura) Spivey, Madison (husband, Derek) Way and Josh Spivey; great-grandson, Ryder Spivey; and another great-grandson, Zane Way, expected in August; daughter-in-law, Jenny Spivey; and several nieces and nephews. He was preceded in death by his parents and son, Greg Spivey.
Visitation will be Thursday, May 14, 2026, from 4 to 8 p.m. at Murphy-Parks Funeral Service, 703 S. Harrison St., Shelbyville, Indiana 46176. Graveside services will be Friday, May 15, 2026, at 1 p.m. at Fairland Cemetery, 10053 N. 850 W., Fairland, Indiana 46126, with Pastor Max Southern officiating. The family would like to invite guests to show up in casual wear and come as they are. Funeral directors Greg Parks, Sheila Parks and Stuart Parks are honored to serve Herman’s family. Online condolences may be shared at murphyparks.com.
